newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli ex-army chief aims at top political job.
newsitem.headline: Israeli ex-army chief aims at top political job.

text.p: Former Israeli army chief Ehud Barak on Monday launched a bid to take the reins of the opposition Labour party from Shimon Peres, the seasoned warrior's first step on a path towards Israel's top job.
Long touted as a future prime minister, Barak, 54, like his slain mentor Yitzhak Rabin, combines a vaunted military record with a daring demeanor popular among Israelis.
Barak has cast himself as a Labour centrist, distancing himself from Peres and Haim Ramon, a former cabinet minister also expected to declare candidacy for the premiership.
As Israel's top soldier Barak oversaw the first handover of occupied land to the Palestinians in Gaza and Jericho under a 1994 peace deal with the PLO.
The army chief hung up his uniform after 35 years of service in January of 1995 before joining the Labour party. He was appointed interior minister in Rabin's government the following July.
After Rabin was assassinated last November by a Jew opposed to swapping occupied land for peace with the Palestinians, Barak became foreign minister in the government of Peres.

Like his Labour party comrades, Barak unexpectedly found himself in the opposition when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defeated Peres by less than a percentage point in Israeli elections last May.

A former commando who took part in undercover missions in Arab states, Barak is famous for a 1973 foray into Beirut in which three PLO leaders were killed to avenge the murders of 11 Israeli athletes at the 1972 Munich Olympics.
Israeli news reports said Barak escaped posing as a woman.

Military sources say Barak devised many of the army's tactics against the Palestinian uprising which erupted in 1987, targeting leading militants rather than trying to crush the revolt with unrestrained force.

Authors Dan Raviv and Yossi Melman wrote in their book, Every Spy a Prince, that Barak directed Israel's April 1988 raid on a Tunis suburb to kill PLO military commander Abu Jihad, believed to have been coordinating the uprising.
While army chief in 1994, Barak met his Syrian counterpart for security talks in Washington that proved unproductive. He also played a key role in clinching a peace treaty with Jordan.
Barak was later dogged by media accusations -- which he vehemently denied -- that he ignored wounded troops during a 1992 training incident in which five soldiers were killed and six wounded.
